log: DOES 0.688 TRANSFER TO THE REACTIONS BEING FILLED?
The benchmark is 400 solved reactions with the answer hidden. The deliverable is 9,186 that
were never solved. Different populations, so the accuracy has to be transferred, not assumed.
RETRIEVAL DEPTH
population                     mean  starved <12    zero
benchmark (400 solved)          7.8       47.5%   11.8%
real orphans (4000 sampled)     4.8       70.8%   35.0%
THE CONFOUND, which flattened the first projection I made and made it wrong.
example count        n  obscure share  median lit bin  accuracy
Reactions with NO examples are the MOST-studied ones, so their high accuracy is closed-book
knowledge rather than retrieval. Averaging over that cell imports a score earned by fame
onto a population that has none, and it is what made the flat aggregate look reassuring.

READING
On the 40% of orphans whose retrieval depth HAS been measured on obscure reactions
at usable sample size, the projected top-1 is 0.709 against a headline of 0.688.
BUT 60% OF THE DELIVERABLE IS NOT COVERED BY ANY USABLE CELL, so this projection
describes a minority of the rows and must not be quoted as the table's accuracy. The
honest statement is that the transfer CANNOT be established from this benchmark: the
cells that matter are either unmeasured or too thin, and that is a fact about the
benchmark's design, not about the method.
The other 60% sit in a cell with no obscure measurement at all -- the benchmark
contains no obscure reaction with zero examples, because a solved reaction almost always
has chemical neighbours while a genuine orphan often does not. That share is reported as
UNKNOWN and not averaged in; a mean over an unmeasured cell is a guess with a decimal point.
PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: n_examples is the single best triage field in the review table, and
it is already there. Sort by it. Full-retrieval rows are worth reviewing first; zero-example
rows are unvalidated territory and should be treated as leads, not predictions.
